channel.title: Signal Brief · Cybersecurity
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: Check Point zero-day chained with PHP2Shell to wipe VMware hosts
item.description: Check Point has released emergency hotfixes for a zero-day privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039, that attackers have exploited against a couple of dozen customers since late October. Attackers first entered through Mobile Access portals using the PHP2Shell flaws, then used the flaw to run commands as root, installed the TSGA backdoor, and in an early wave wiped VMware ESXi hosts. The company advises customers who cannot patch immediately to stop the DynamicCLI daemon as a temporary mitigation. Why it matters for tech: A chained portal flaw plus a root escalation shows how one unpatched gateway can become a route to destructive attacks on virtualisation hosts.

item.title: FBI says North Korean hackers stole over $400 million in deepfake video call scheme
item.description: The FBI says North Korean hackers stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over 18 months through a scheme it calls FaceStealer, which lures targets into fake video meetings that play recorded webcam footage of people they trust. Once on the call, victims are told of a fake audio fault and sent a link that installs malware to steal wallets and credentials. US authorities seized the cloud infrastructure behind the scheme and more than 900 recorded victim videos, and the Justice Department separately won court approval to seize or restrain over $1.2 billion stolen from Binance by a different North Korean group. Why it matters for tech: The scheme turns a victim's own face into the lure for the next target, so verifying meeting invitations through a second channel matters more than ever.

item.title: Operation Endgame seizes servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC
item.description: An international police operation has taken down servers behind the Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC malware tools, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains and about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims. Gootloader spread through fake legal documents on hacked websites and was used in ransomware attacks, while CastleRAT gave attackers remote control of infected machines and StealC stole passwords. Dutch police have loaded data stolen by CastleRAT into their Check your hack service so people can see if their email address was affected. Why it matters for tech: Taking down the loaders and stealers that feed ransomware cuts off the access brokers' supply chain, even when no arrests are announced.

item.title: Trezor confirms hardware implants in three wallets and cuts reseller network
item.description: Trezor has confirmed that three Safe 5 hardware wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained hidden circuit boards designed to steal recovery phrases and send them to attackers over a mobile network. The company released firmware 2.13.1 on November 11, which stops the implants from capturing anything on screen, and says no affected customer has reported losing funds. Trezor has also cut its global reseller network by about 80 percent and is offering replacement devices to anyone who bought a wallet from CryptoBilis since March 2026. Why it matters for tech: A hardware wallet is only as trustworthy as its supply chain, so a tampered device shows why buying from authorised sellers matters.

item.title: Apache patches a critical HTTP/2 flaw that allows remote code execution
item.description: The Apache Software Foundation has fixed a critical race condition in the mod_http2 module of Apache HTTP Server, tracked as CVE-2026-119618, which an unauthenticated attacker could exploit to gain remote code execution. The flaw affects HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner and Google Cloud's Vulnerability Research teams. Cloud security company Wiz reports that 64% of cloud environments hold vulnerable resources, though the flaw needs HTTP/2 enabled, which is off by default, and no public exploit is known. Why it matters for tech: Apache still serves about one in five websites, so a remotely exploitable flaw in its HTTP/2 code is a patch-now item for anyone running it.

item.title: New SignDrop zero-day turns a Windows security mitigation into a privilege escalation
item.description: Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri has disclosed SignDrop, a Windows zero-day that abuses the Common Log File System mitigations Microsoft added in October 2025. The flaw lets an attacker trick a privileged process, such as an antivirus engine, into creating an authentication file with SYSTEM privileges, which can then be used to turn off antivirus and endpoint protection. Naceri tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, estimates 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable, and says there is no fix yet except waiting for a Microsoft patch. Why it matters for tech: A defence that can be turned against itself is a reminder that mitigations need their own review, and defenders cannot patch this one yet.

item.title: Maersk confirms a breach of a legacy logistics system as a ransomware gang demands $5 million
item.description: Maersk has confirmed that a threat actor breached a local legacy system from its acquired LF Logistics arm and stole data. The WhiteArmor ransomware gang claims about 100GB of data and demands $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. Maersk says the incident is isolated to that system, current evidence shows no sensitive data has been disclosed, and operations are unaffected. Why it matters for tech: The breach hit a system inherited through acquisition, which is a reminder that acquired infrastructure carries its own exposure long after the deal closes.

item.title: More than 35,000 Grok-built apps found open online, some leaking confidential data
item.description: Security researchers at Claroc found 37,571 Grok-built apps online, of which 35,578 were open to anyone without signing in. About one in ten contained internal business or personal data, and roughly 2% of the open apps held material rated high or critical. Twenty-four of the apps were built by staff at X and SpaceX, including a confidential sales onboarding plan, and the company has since taken those staff apps down. Why it matters for tech: Apps built by typing a description inherit the builder's sharing default, so a tool meant for quick prototypes can quietly publish internal data.

item.title: CISA adds an exploited Cisco BroadWorks flaw to its must-patch list
item.description: CISA has added CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity flaw in Cisco BroadWorks that lets remote attackers read sensitive configuration, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Federal civilian agencies must patch by November 24, and CISA urges private organisations to prioritise it too. Cisco patched the flaw in August, and threat researchers report it was exploited with help from a jailbroken AI model in attacks on a European telecom provider. Why it matters for tech: A patched flaw becomes urgent once exploitation is confirmed, and the reported AI-assisted attack shows how quickly a known bug can be turned into a live intrusion.

item.title: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixes 1,235 flaws, including an exploited Outlook zero-day
item.description: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday addresses 1,235 vulnerabilities, including 66 rated Critical, with one actively exploited zero-day in Outlook. The zero-day, CVE-2026-124194, is a spoofing flaw in which opening a specially crafted message file can make Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, disclosing the user's NTLMv2 hash. Microsoft rates the flaw Moderate with a CVSS score of 6.5, and CISA added it to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalog on November 10 with a November 24 patching deadline for federal agencies. Why it matters for tech: A single crafted message file can expose credentials used to impersonate a user, so the fix matters for any organisation running Outlook, and the federal deadline sets the pace for patching.

item.title: Attackers exploit a Xen Orchestra authentication bypass to seize virtualisation hosts
item.description: Vates has warned that a critical authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra, tracked as VSA-2026-062, is being actively exploited in the wild. A specially crafted cookie can bypass login and give an attacker administrative actions, leading to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full takeover of an XCP-ng node as root. Vates linked the activity to an IP address previously flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control server. Fixed versions are Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0, and xo-server 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. Why it matters for tech: Xen Orchestra manages virtual machines and server pools, so a login bypass on an internet-facing instance hands an attacker the control plane for the hosts behind it.

item.title: SAP patches four maximum-severity flaws, including two that allow remote code execution
item.description: SAP's November Security Patch Day addresses 38 new vulnerabilities, nine of them rated Critical, with four carrying the maximum CVSS score of 10.0. The four cover a SAML assertion verification bypass in NetWeaver AS ABAP, memory corruption in the Internet Communication Manager, a default access-control setting in SAP Gateway, and a heap overflow in SAP Web Dispatcher. SAP has not reported active exploitation of the four, and none of them appears in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities catalog. Why it matters for tech: Four maximum-severity flaws in core SAP systems, two of them leading to remote code execution, make patching a priority this week for teams running SAP, even with no exploitation reported yet.

item.title: N-able takes its N-central platform offline after 30 alleged zero-days surface
item.description: N-able has taken its hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific and told customers running the software on site to shut down their servers, after researcher Sean Bales disclosed more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in a GitHub repository named Able2Shell. The flaws include authentication bypass, credential disclosure and remote code execution, and the most critical chain used unauthenticated XXE to steal a session, reset a password and run commands as the nable user. N-able said it had not observed active exploitation and is developing a hotfix, with updates every four hours and no return-to-service estimate given. Why it matters for tech: N-central manages IT systems for many small and mid-sized businesses, so taking the platform offline shows how a single disclosure can halt remote management for a large customer base at once.

item.title: SSHole flaw lets attackers bypass login on some Linux systems
item.description: A flaw named SSHole allows authentication bypass in OpenSSH on certain Linux systems built on musl, including Alpine, for accounts whose password hash is the single character "*". An oversized password makes musl return "*", which OpenSSH then treats as a match. Exploitation began on November 5, the day a proof of concept appeared, and OpenSSH 10.6p2 was released the same day as the fix. GreyNoise recorded the first successful exploitation on November 7, with 16 successful chains from 6 source IP addresses. Why it matters for tech: The flaw turns a password length check into a login bypass on affected systems, so administrators running musl-based Linux need the patched OpenSSH version rather than relying on password strength.

item.title: Iris Ohyama breach may have exposed data of 7.7 million people
item.description: Japanese manufacturer Iris Ohyama said personal information belonging to about 7.7 million people may have been exposed after unauthorised access to a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza online store. The company said the impact reaches up to 5.8 million registered and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth and passwords may have been exposed, though passwords for active members were stored encrypted and card data was not in the affected service. As of November 5 the company had received no reports of misuse, and Japan's privacy regulator and police were notified on October 29. Why it matters for tech: A breach through a supplier's cloud service shows customer data can be exposed even when the retailer's own systems are not the entry point.

item.title: Claude Code settings files leak passwords and keys in public GitHub repos
item.description: Security researchers at Apiiro found 1,122 public copies of Claude Code's settings file holding at least one secret, including database passwords, cloud keys and tokens. The file, .claude/settings.local.json, records commands a user approved with 'don't ask again', word for word, so passwords typed into a command are saved in plain text. Apiiro counted 1,379 secrets in current copies and 2,539 in total across 1,994 repositories once older versions, forks and shared settings files are included, and says the fix starts with rotating every exposed credential. Why it matters for tech: Secrets saved in agent settings files leak into public repos, so teams need to treat agent folders like credential stores and scan their history.

item.title: French bank Arkéa hit by heist of up to $133 million through a service provider
item.description: French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was hit by a cyberattack in which the attacker used the bank's own account to send fraudulent transactions to other banks. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT estimated up to 118 million euros ($133 million) was taken and converted into stablecoins, while the bank would only confirm the order of magnitude. The bank says customer assets were not affected, the incident is closed and under control, and it is working with police to establish how the attacker got in through a service provider's platform. Why it matters for tech: A bank's own account was used to move funds through a service provider, showing third-party access is now a direct route to the money.

item.title: Microsoft warns agentic AI framework ARTEX is being used against banks
item.description: Microsoft says the financially motivated group it tracks as Storm-3358 began targeting financial organisations in October using ARTEX, an agentic AI offensive framework. The group, which Microsoft describes as Cambodia-based and focused on financial targets in Southeast Asia, uses ARTEX agents to scan public systems, exploit flaws such as anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery, and install remote access trojans. Microsoft has published indicators of compromise and detections, and says defenders need AI-assisted investigation to match attacks that move at machine speed. Why it matters for tech: Agentic frameworks let attackers scan, exploit and move laterally at machine speed, so defence has to detect and respond at the same pace.

item.title: Chainalysis breach exposed credentials for all customers
item.description: Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says an attack on its systems exposed usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all of its customers. The company, whose customers include law enforcement, government agencies and financial institutions, has taken its login portal and several products offline, including Reactor and its transaction screening tools. It says it has found no evidence that investigation data was accessed, and all users will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys before regaining access. Why it matters for tech: A breach at a firm that traces crypto crime puts its own customers’ access at risk, and the shutdown shows how much trust the service carries.

item.title: QNAP warns hackers are breaching NAS devices through Plex
item.description: QNAP says hackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell chain of four flaws in Plex Media Server to compromise its network attached storage devices, and it has received multiple reports of suspected breaches. The company urges users to update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3.10861 through the QNAP App Center, noting that its own operating systems are not affected. Users with an exposed Plex server should treat their device and stored content as compromised, check for signs of intrusion and reinstall the operating system rather than only updating. Why it matters for tech: A media app flaw is reaching into home and small business storage, and updating alone will not clear an attack that has already landed.

item.title: OpenSSH ships emergency fix for a flaw that let long passwords bypass login on Alpine Linux
item.description: OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 to fix a critical flaw in which a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long could log in to accounts with no password set, such as key only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers. The flaw affects systems where the server checks passwords without PAM, which is how Alpine's openssh-server package is built. Alpine published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16, and no attacks using the flaw have been reported. Why it matters for tech: A password check that accepts the wrong input is a serious failure, and Alpine's wide use in containers makes fast patching matter.

item.title: FBI and CISA warn hackers are targeting refrigeration systems
item.description: The FBI and CISA warned that hackers are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems worldwide, in a joint advisory with the US health, agriculture and transport departments. Attackers exploit unpatched or internet accessible temperature controllers to alter settings, which can spoil food, damage equipment and create fire hazards. The warning follows attacks on European refrigeration systems, including controllers at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets in October. Why it matters for tech: Cyberattacks on refrigeration reach beyond data theft into food safety and public health, so operators are urged to take controllers off the public internet.

item.description: Zyxel has patched a zero day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches. BleepingComputer reports that attackers exploited it to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. Why it matters for tech: Network switches are trusted infrastructure; stolen configurations hand attackers a map of the networks those switches protect.

item.title: Google patches critical Android flaw that needs no user interaction
item.description: Google's November security bulletin patches a critical flaw, CVE-2026-58868, that could let an attacker run code on a phone remotely without any user action. It affects Android 14 through 17, and the fix arrives at security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers distribute on their own schedules. Why it matters for tech: The gap between Google's patch and each maker's rollout is the window of exposure for most Android users.

item.title: Microsoft tracks fake download campaign spreading trojanised installers
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence is tracking a campaign that uses trojanised Inno installers, spread through fake download pages, to deliver monetisation payloads. Microsoft published detection and investigation guidance covering the complete installer session. Why it matters for tech: Fake installers remain one of the most reliable ways attackers reach ordinary users and company machines.

item.title: Microsoft: real world exploitation concentrates in a small set of vulnerabilities
item.description: Microsoft's analysis of real world attacks finds that exploitation concentrates in a small, high impact subset of known vulnerabilities. It advises defenders to prioritise patching by exploitation likelihood, exposure and potential blast radius, rather than by severity score alone. Why it matters for tech: It gives security teams an evidence based order for patching when they cannot patch everything at once.
